title: Orbit Workshop
subject: Physics
summary: Compare collisions, orbits and escapes by changing one launch variable at a time.
question: How does sideways launch speed change a falling path?
explanation: Gravity accelerates a probe toward the central body while sideways motion carries it forward. At one starting radius in this model, too little sideways speed intersects the drawn surface, the baseline speed makes a circular orbit, and at least √2 times that baseline escapes. Doubling central mass raises the circular speed to √2 times the original baseline, so an unchanged launch curves into a tighter ellipse. Gravity continues to act along bound and escape paths.

experiments.title: Change sideways speed
experiments.instruction: Predict the sequence for 0.60×, 1.00× and 1.42× launch speed. Keep central mass at 1× and the starting radius fixed, then compare all three traces.
experiments.observe: Identify collision, bound orbit and escape. Explain why the escaping trace still curves while gravity acts.

experiments.title: Change central mass
experiments.instruction: Predict the path at 2× central mass. Keep launch speed at 1.00× and the starting radius fixed, then compare with mass 1×.
experiments.observe: Compare the displayed 1.00–1.00 and 0.33–1.00 trace ranges. Explain why the same launch no longer makes a circle.

misconception: Escape does not mean gravity switches off. Gravity weakens with distance and keeps curving the escape path even though it cannot turn the probe back.

title: Light Bending Studio
subject: Physics
summary: Compare reflection and refraction, then find when a higher-index material keeps a ray inside.
question: How do angle and travel direction change a ray at a boundary?
explanation: Reflection stays in the first medium and leaves at the incident angle. Refraction crosses the boundary; Snell’s law relates both angles to the materials’ refractive indices. Refractive index compares light’s speed in vacuum with its speed in a material, so a higher index means slower light. Measure every angle from the normal, the line perpendicular to the boundary. Entering a higher index bends a slanting ray toward the normal; entering a lower index bends it away. Above the critical angle, a higher-to-lower-index ray undergoes total internal reflection.

experiments.title: Cross the critical angle
experiments.instruction: Keep glass to air fixed. Predict whether a transmitted ray remains when only the incident angle changes from 40° to 43°.
experiments.observe: Compare the 40° transmitted ray with its absence at 43°. Relate the change to the 41.8° critical angle.

experiments.title: Reverse the boundary
experiments.instruction: Keep the incident angle at 30°. Predict how the refracted ray changes between air to glass and glass to air.
experiments.observe: Compare the 19.5° and 48.6° refracted angles while the reflected angle remains 30°. Explain toward-versus-away bending.

misconception: A ray does not totally reflect merely because it meets a boundary. Total internal reflection requires travel from higher to lower refractive index and an incident angle above that pair’s critical angle.

title: Gravity Drop Lab
subject: Physics
summary: Compare how object mass and local gravity affect a vacuum drop.
question: What changes a vacuum drop: object mass or local gravity?
explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object; weight is the gravitational force on it. In a vacuum at one location, objects released together from the same height have the same acceleration regardless of mass. Changing local gravity changes acceleration and weight, while mass stays fixed. This near-surface model uses constant local gravity.

experiments.title: Change only mass
experiments.instruction: Keep Earth gravity and a 20 m release height fixed. Predict which lands first, then compare 1 kg with 10 kg.
experiments.observe: Both land in 2.02 s, while their weights are 9.81 N and 98.1 N. Explain why weight changes but vacuum acceleration does not.

experiments.title: Change only local gravity
experiments.instruction: Keep mass at 5 kg and the release height at 20 m. Predict which drop takes longer, then compare Earth with the Moon.
experiments.observe: Earth takes 2.02 s and the Moon takes 4.97 s. Explain why weaker local gravity changes the fall while mass stays fixed.

misconception: More weight does not produce more free-fall acceleration when gravity is the only force: the added gravitational force and added inertia scale together. Air resistance can change real-world results.

title: Solar System Explorer
subject: Space science
summary: Compare the eight planets at equal elapsed time and on one diameter scale.
question: What changes when planets are compared for the same elapsed time or on the same diameter scale?
explanation: The Sun’s gravity keeps eight planets in orbit. A year is one planet’s complete orbit, so planets with different orbital periods complete different fractions in the same elapsed time. One astronomical unit (AU) is about Earth’s mean distance from the Sun. Planet diameters and Sun–planet gaps differ so greatly that a useful screen model must show them on separate scales.

experiments.title: Hold elapsed time fixed
experiments.instruction: Predict whether Earth, Neptune or both complete the same orbit fraction in one Earth year. Select your prediction, then compare one Earth year.
experiments.observe: Earth completes 1.000 orbit and Neptune about 0.006 orbit (1/165). Explain why equal elapsed time does not mean equal orbital fractions.

experiments.title: Hold diameter scale fixed
experiments.instruction: Predict whether Jupiter is about 5, 11 or 50 Earth diameters across. Select your prediction, then compare Earth and Jupiter.
experiments.observe: Jupiter’s equatorial diameter is about 11.21 Earth diameters. Explain why a separately framed close-up cannot establish this ratio.

misconception: A convenient orbit picture does not show true planet sizes and true gaps on one common scale. The model’s circular paths and starting positions are illustrative, not today’s sky.

title: Moon Phase Observatory
subject: Space science
summary: Change the Moon’s orbital position and compare the sunlit fraction seen from Earth with the Sun–Earth–Moon geometry.
question: How does the Moon’s position around Earth change the phase we see?
explanation: The Sun illuminates half the Moon. As the Moon travels around Earth, our viewpoint reveals changing portions of that sunlit hemisphere. The mean phase cycle from new Moon to new Moon is about 29.53 days, not the 27.32-day sidereal orbit relative to the stars. The model uses a circular, coplanar orbit with enlarged objects and gaps; it does not predict local sky orientation, libration, eclipses, terrain shadows, or exact timing.

experiments.title: Test first quarter
experiments.instruction: Predict whether 25%, 50%, or 75% of the Earth-view disk will look lit at 90°. Keep the Sun direction and Earth viewpoint fixed, then observe first quarter.
experiments.observe: The visible disk is 50% lit. Explain how half the visible disk differs from half the whole Moon always receiving sunlight.

experiments.title: Compare opposite quarters
experiments.instruction: Predict whether first quarter at 90° or last quarter at 270° has a larger visible lit fraction. Compare them from the same Earth viewpoint.
experiments.observe: Both disks are 50% lit, on opposite sides. Explain why equal fractions can have different phase names without Earth’s shadow.

misconception: The usual Moon phases are not Earth’s shadow. Earth’s shadow causes a lunar eclipse, a separate event that does not happen every month.

title: Leaf Energy Lab
subject: Biology
summary: Test why extra light cannot replace water or carbon dioxide in photosynthesis.
question: Can extra light replace water as an input to photosynthesis?
explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide. The released oxygen comes from water. One required input cannot replace another, and real responses depend on more than this activity’s invented settings. Plants also respire day and night.

experiments.title: Test a missing input
experiments.instruction: Hold water at 0% and carbon dioxide at 80%. Predict, then compare 30% and 100% light.
experiments.observe: Both toy activity indices remain zero because light energy cannot replace water.

experiments.title: Find the limiting input
experiments.instruction: Hold water at 35% and carbon dioxide at 80%. Predict, then compare 15%, 35% and 100% light.
experiments.observe: The index rises until water ties with, then limits, the model’s response.

misconception: Plants do not absorb sugar food from soil. Light supplies energy; water and carbon dioxide supply matter used to make sugars.

title: Castle Design Lab
subject: History
summary: Test how a gate, ditch and projecting tower change routes and wall-side views.
question: How did separate defenses change an approach to a stone castle?
explanation: This 13th-century English-inspired composite is not a reconstruction of one castle. Gatehouses controlled passage, ditches interrupted approaches, projecting towers changed viewing positions along wall faces, and multiple wall lines could add successive barriers. Castles also housed households, workers and administrators. Designs varied by period, site, terrain and resources; this controlled model compares routes and illustrated viewing directions, not weapon ranges or the outcome of a siege.

experiments.title: Compare two open-gate routes
experiments.instruction: Keep the gate open and ditch at 22 m. Predict which routes reach an entrance, compare the bridge route with the north-wall route, then inspect both endpoints.
experiments.observe: The bridge reaches the entrance; the north route stops at the ditch. Explain why opening one gate does not remove a ditch or create a doorway through another wall.

experiments.title: Compare wall-side viewpoints
experiments.instruction: Keep the bridge route, closed gate and 22 m ditch fixed. Predict which position shows more adjoining wall faces, then compare the flat corner with the projecting tower.
experiments.observe: Count the dashed viewing directions in both trials. Explain why projecting beyond a wall changes what can be seen; the lines are illustrative directions, not complete visibility or weapon ranges.

misconception: No single feature made a castle impregnable. Not every castle had stone walls, a keep, concentric defenses or a water-filled moat; ditches could be dry, and designs changed over centuries.

title: Sound Playground
subject: Physics
summary: Predict and compare how string length and modeled midpoint displacement change frequency.
question: How can two plucks keep the same modeled frequency while their midpoint displacement amplitudes differ?
explanation: Frequency counts cycles per second and strongly influences perceived pitch, but frequency and pitch are not identical. For this ideal uniform string’s fixed-end fundamental, doubling length while holding tension and mass per length fixed halves frequency. Doubling the modeled midpoint displacement does not change that natural frequency; it quadruples an A² comparison index. That index is not a decibel or loudness reading. No acoustic radiation is calculated. Real musical sounds also depend on harmonics, the instrument body and how the sound changes over time.

experiments.title: Compare string lengths
experiments.instruction: Keep tension and midpoint displacement fixed. Predict what happens when vibrating length doubles from 60 to 120 cm, then run the fixed comparison.
experiments.observe: The longer trial has half as many cycles per second. Use the unchanged-variable list to explain why length caused the difference.

experiments.title: Compare midpoint displacements
experiments.instruction: Keep length and tension fixed. Predict whether changing modeled displacement from 3 to 6 mm changes frequency, then run the fixed comparison.
experiments.observe: Frequency stays the same while midpoint displacement and the relative A² index change. Explain why this is not a loudness measurement.

misconception: A larger modeled string displacement is not automatically a higher pitch or a direct loudness reading. Frequency strongly influences pitch; perceived loudness depends on sound level, frequency, hearing and listening conditions.

title: Bridge Builder
subject: Engineering
summary: Move one static point load and compare support reactions, bending moment and modeled beam deflection.
question: How do load position and load size change the forces and bending of a simply supported beam?
explanation: Static equilibrium requires the upward support reactions to equal the downward point load and their torques to balance. Moving the load changes how the two supports share it. This activity also calculates peak bending moment and small deflection for a 10 m equivalent beam with a fixed flexural rigidity EI. The timber truss is explanatory artwork, not the structure being solved. Brace buttons change only an invented comparison index; they do not calculate truss forces, member capacity or a safe load.

experiments.title: Move the same load
experiments.instruction: Keep the 10 m span, 12 kN point load, 100 MN·m² flexural rigidity and brace index fixed. Predict which support carries more when the load moves from the center to 20% of the span, then compare both trials.
experiments.observe: At the center, both reactions are 6.0 kN. At 20%, the left reaction is 9.6 kN and the right is 2.4 kN; peak moment and deflection at the load are also smaller. Explain how force and torque balance support this result.

experiments.title: Double the point load
experiments.instruction: Keep the load at midspan, the 10 m span, 100 MN·m² flexural rigidity and brace index fixed. Predict what happens to peak moment and deflection when the point load changes from 8 to 16 kN, then compare.
experiments.observe: Peak moment changes from 20.0 to 40.0 kN·m and deflection at the load changes from 1.67 to 3.33 mm. Explain why both double in this linear beam model and why that does not identify a safe load.

misconception: A triangular frame or a low teaching index does not prove that a bridge is safe. Real design also checks member forces, connections, shear, buckling, fatigue, impact, wind, material limits, safety factors and other loads.

title: River Sculptor
subject: Earth science
summary: Compare vegetation and slope, then account for soil that stays, deposits or exits downstream.
question: How do vegetation and catchment slope change runoff and soil transport in this model?
explanation: Water erosion detaches and transports soil. Sediment can settle where flow slows or continue downstream. Vegetation and stable soil structure can increase infiltration and reduce runoff, while long, steep slopes can increase the power of water to erode and transport soil. This one-hour, one-hectare teaching model holds many real conditions fixed so you can compare one variable at a time. Its runoff, erosion, export and channel-capacity coefficients are invented; the results are not field measurements or a flood forecast.

experiments.title: Add vegetation
experiments.instruction: Predict what happens to runoff and soil export when vegetation changes from 0% to 100%. Compare one 40 mm storm on an 8% slope with the same 5,000 kg starting soil, area and duration.
experiments.observe: Compare runoff, infiltration, soil moved, deposition and export in both trials. Which changes explain the smaller or larger downstream export?

experiments.title: Steepen the slope
experiments.instruction: Predict whether runoff, soil moved or both change when catchment slope changes from 2% to 20%. Compare one storm with rain fixed at 40 mm, vegetation fixed at 40% and the same 5,000 kg starting soil, area and duration.
experiments.observe: Runoff stays fixed in this teaching formula while soil moved and export increase. Explain why this result describes the model relationship rather than every real catchment.

misconception: Erosion does not destroy soil. Removed material is transported, then deposits within the reach or exits downstream. Clearer water can still mean sediment settled elsewhere.

sources.title: USGS: Sediment and suspended sediment

title: Circuit City
subject: Physics
summary: Compare one series path with parallel branches, then measure how voltage changes current, power and energy.
question: How do circuit paths and source voltage control charge flow and energy transfer?
explanation: Current is charge flow rate (A = C/s), voltage is energy transferred per charge (V = J/C), and power is energy-transfer rate (W = J/s). For each fixed 12 Ω resistor in this ideal direct-current model, V = IR and P = VI. The same current passes through every load in series, while parallel branch currents add at the source. Charge is conserved around a complete circuit; the source transfers energy to the loads. The model uses an ideal 0–18 V source, zero-resistance wires and fixed resistors. It omits heating, transients, source sag, component limits and protective devices and is not guidance for household mains wiring.

experiments.title: Open one switch
experiments.instruction: Predict the effect of opening house 2. Compare series and parallel at the same ideal 12 V source, with houses 1 and 3 closed and all three resistors fixed at 12 Ω.
experiments.observe: Series source current is 0 A because the only path is open. In parallel, houses 1 and 3 each carry 1 A and transfer 12 W while house 2 carries 0 A. Explain which paths remain complete.

experiments.title: Double the voltage
experiments.instruction: Predict what changes when the ideal source increases from 6 V to 12 V. Keep all switches closed, use parallel wiring, keep each resistor fixed at 12 Ω and observe both trials for 10 s.
experiments.observe: Each branch changes from 0.5 A, 3 W and 30 J to 1 A, 12 W and 120 J. Use I = V/R and P = V²/R to explain why current doubles while power and energy quadruple.

misconception: A load does not use up charge. Charge returns to the source while energy is transferred from the source to the loads; moving markers show conventional-current direction, not individual charges or their drift speed.

sources.title: OpenStax College Physics 2e: Resistors in Series and Parallel

title: Food Web Rescue
subject: Biology
summary: Predict how removing fish or increasing nutrients changes a bounded pond model, then compare controlled trials.
question: Can adding more nutrients make conditions worse for fish?
explanation: Algae capture light energy, zooplankton graze algae, and fish can eat zooplankton. Food-web arrows point from resource or prey toward consumer because they trace energy flow; they do not show organisms moving. This chain is one path inside a larger web, so changing a consumer can affect a producer indirectly. Added nutrients can support algal growth, while respiration and decomposition can consume dissolved oxygen. The model uses invented 0–100 population, nutrient, oxygen and detritus indices, illustrative weekly steps and uncalibrated coefficients. It is designed to show qualitative interactions, not to forecast a real pond. Temperature, light, mixing, nutrient form, daily oxygen cycles, species differences and many other processes are omitted.

experiments.title: Remove a consumer
experiments.instruction: Predict what changes when fish are absent. Compare 6 illustrative weeks with fish present versus fish absent. Hold nutrient supply at index 50, drought at 0%, and the algae, zooplankton, oxygen and detritus starting indices fixed.
experiments.observe: The fish-absent trial finishes with a higher zooplankton index and lower algae index in this model. Use the resource-to-consumer links to explain the indirect response, and identify the changed and held variables.

experiments.title: Increase nutrient supply
experiments.instruction: Predict what changes from nutrient index 20 to 100. Compare 8 illustrative weeks while holding drought at 60%, keeping every population present, and using the same algae, zooplankton, fish, oxygen and detritus starting indices.
experiments.observe: The high-nutrient trial finishes with higher algae and detritus indices but lower oxygen and fish indices in this model. Explain why more nutrients do not guarantee that every index rises, without treating the values as a field forecast.

misconception: Food-web arrows do not show which way animals travel; they point from resource or prey to consumer to trace energy flow. A web is not a ladder where only the top animal matters, and more nutrients do not necessarily improve conditions for every organism.

title: Fraction Feast
subject: Mathematics
summary: Hold the whole area fixed, compare equal partitions and add fractions with an exact shared unit.
question: How do piece size and piece count work together when fractions are equivalent or added?
explanation: A fraction describes equal parts of a whole. The denominator tells how many equal pieces make that whole; the numerator counts selected pieces. Comparisons are fair only when the wholes have the same area. One half and two quarters cover the same amount because doubling the piece count makes each piece half as large. To add fractions with different denominators, first rename both portions with a common-sized piece. The exact total may be greater than one whole.

experiments.title: Different pieces, same portion
experiments.instruction: Keep the whole area and selected area fixed. Show 1/2 on plate A, predict what changes when every piece is split in two, then compare with 2/4.
experiments.observe: The selected piece count doubles while each piece becomes half as large; 1/2 and 2/4 cover the same area. Explain why changing both numerator and denominator by the same factor preserves the amount.

experiments.title: Combine unlike pieces
experiments.instruction: Use equal-area wholes. Select 2/3 and 3/4, predict whether their sum fits in one whole, then combine the portions using equal twelfths.
experiments.observe: The exact conversion is 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12, or 1 whole and 5/12. Explain why the numerators add while the common denominator stays 12.

misconception: A larger denominator does not automatically mean more food. With the same whole and numerator, more equal parts make each selected part smaller.

title: Pattern Palace
subject: Mathematics
summary: Compare a quarter-turn with a reflection, then calculate how regular-polygon corners fit around one point.
question: What changes when a motif is turned or reflected, and when does a regular-polygon corner total fill 360°?
explanation: A rotation turns every point through the same angle around a center. A reflection maps points across a line. Both are rigid transformations, so corresponding lengths and angles stay equal, but a reflection reverses orientation while a rotation does not. Around one point, regular-polygon interior angles must total 360° to meet without a local gap or overlap. This corner calculation is evidence about that point; one finite arrangement alone is not proof that a proposed rule continues across the whole plane.

experiments.title: Turn or flip?
experiments.instruction: Keep the asymmetric motif, center and marked point M fixed. Predict whether a 90° clockwise turn or a reflection across the vertical line moves M farther right, then compare both images.
experiments.observe: The turn puts M 18 units right and 30 units up; the reflection puts M 30 units right and 18 units up. Explain how the positions differ even though corresponding lengths and angles stay equal.

experiments.title: Fill a full turn
experiments.instruction: Keep the regular-pentagon shape, side length, 108° interior angle and meeting point fixed. Three corners leave 36°. Predict what happens when a fourth pentagon is added, then compare both totals.
experiments.observe: Three corners total 324° and leave 36°; four total 432° and overlap by 72°. Explain why adding a whole 108° corner cannot fill only the 36° gap.

misconception: Seeing a 360° fit at one corner is not by itself proof that a proposed pattern tiles the plane. The arrangement must continue consistently at every point, and regular and irregular polygons with the same number of sides are not interchangeable.

title: Caravan Crossroads
subject: History
summary: Predict, then compare how changing only season or route affects travel time, delivered cargo, load and margin in a fictional trade model.
question: When every other rule stays fixed, how can one modeled route or season change alter several journey outcomes?
explanation: The historical Silk Roads were overlapping land and sea networks connecting many communities, not one road or a one-way end-to-end journey. Goods, knowledge, skills and ideas moved through local and long-distance exchanges, often changing hands between merchants. This lesson studies two controlled comparisons on one fictional composite segment. Every location, duration, season effect, carrying limit, price, toll, margin, spoilage rule and breakage rule is a teaching assumption, not a historical measurement, probability or forecast.

experiments.title: Change only the season
experiments.instruction: Keep River Road, 6 grain units, 14 supply days, the 100 kg limit and all price and loss rules fixed. Predict whether changing wet season to dry creates more, the same or fewer travel days, then compare the two plans.
experiments.observe: Wet to dry changes 8 to 14 days and 6 to 4 units delivered, while load stays 64 kg. Margin changes from −8 to −22 teaching credits because the invented dry-season rule adds time and crosses the invented grain-spoilage threshold.

experiments.title: Change only the route
experiments.instruction: Keep dry season, 6 pottery units, 12 supply days, the 100 kg limit and all price and loss rules fixed. Predict whether Mountain Pass, Oasis Trail or neither delivers more pottery and keeps the larger margin, then compare.
experiments.observe: Mountain Pass takes 9 days, delivers 5 units and has margin 0. Oasis Trail takes 12 days, delivers 6 units and has margin 15 teaching credits. Both loads stay 66 kg; the longer fictional route avoids the invented breakage rule and has the lower invented toll.

misconception: The Silk Roads were not one road, a simple east-to-west line or a route where the same merchant usually carried goods end to end. Many communities, local exchanges and changing land and sea routes formed the networks.

title: Pollinator Express
subject: Biology
summary: Predict, trace and compare when one modeled bee visit transfers compatible pollen.
question: What can flower visits tell us about pollen transfer—and what can they not tell us?
explanation: Pollinators often visit flowers for nectar or pollen and may move pollen to a flower’s receptive part. That transfer is pollination. Fertilization can happen later after pollen-tube growth and the joining of sperm and egg cells; seed dispersal later moves formed seeds. This deterministic lesson records only pollen transfer. First it changes only the displayed type of one trial flower at one fixed position. Then it changes only whether one bridge habitat patch containing a Gold and a Violet flower is present; the same planned route uses the Gold bridge stop in both conditions. Every coordinate, reach value, flower placement and route is invented for teaching, not an ecological measurement, probability or forecast. Real plants vary in compatibility and self-pollination, and real pollinators can carry mixed pollen.

experiments.title: Change only the trial flower type
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Compare Gold 1 followed by the fixed trial flower set to Gold type with the same route and position set to Violet type. Reach, habitat, coordinates and transfer rule stay fixed.
experiments.observe: Both routes record two visits. Compare one compatible transfer with zero and explain why a visit count alone does not establish compatible pollen transfer.

experiments.title: Bridge a habitat gap
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Attempt the same Gold 1 → Gold 2 → Gold bridge → Gold 3 route at reach 170 with a bridge habitat patch absent and present. The patch contains a Gold and a Violet flower, but the fixed planned route uses only the Gold bridge stop. Only patch presence changes.
experiments.observe: Without the patch, the Gold bridge and Gold 3 attempts are blocked. With it, both succeed. Explain how the Gold stop in the added modeled patch changes route connectivity without treating the result as an ecological forecast.

misconception: A flower visit is not automatically pollination; pollination is not fertilization; and a received-pollen mark does not mean that fruit or seeds formed or dispersed.

title: Chance Carnival
subject: Mathematics
summary: Test how observed results compare with expected chances.
question: Can fair chances give uneven results?
explanation: Expected chance is an outcome’s weight divided by total weight; observed share comes from one sample. Equal weights give equal chances, not equal counts. A zero weight makes an outcome impossible. Larger samples usually settle nearer the expected shares, but a particular larger sample can be farther away. Each computer draw is independent, so a streak does not change the next draw.

experiments.title: Compare sample sizes
experiments.instruction: With four equal weights, predict whether 12 counts must match. Run fresh samples of 12 and 1,200 trials; change only sample size.
experiments.observe: Compare observed percentages with 25% expected for each outcome. Explain uneven counts and why one larger sample can still be farther from 25%.

experiments.title: Double one weight
experiments.instruction: Set weights to 2, 1, 1, 1. Predict whether outcome 1 is 40% (2 of 5) or 50% (2 of 4), then run 200 trials.
experiments.observe: Compare outcome 1’s observed percentage with 40% expected. Explain why doubling one weight also changes total weight.

misconception: Past draws do not make an outcome “due”; independent draws keep the same chances while weights stay fixed.

sources.title: Illustrative Mathematics: Models and observed frequencies

title: Machine Workshop
subject: Engineering
summary: Compare ideal pulleys and a gear winch while holding the load and lift fixed.
question: How can a machine reduce input force without reducing the energy transferred to a lifted load?
explanation: Mass is measured in kilograms. In this model, weight is the force of gravity on that mass, calculated in newtons with a fixed gravitational field strength of 9.81 N/kg. Ideal mechanical advantage compares load force with input force and input travel with load travel. Supporting rope sections share a pulley load; a gear ratio compares driven teeth with driver teeth. For the same slow lift, an ideal machine trades less input force for more input travel, so ideal input work equals the load's gravitational energy gain. Real friction and flexing require extra input energy, so real efficiency is below 100%.

experiments.title: Change only supporting sections
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Keep the load at 40 kg and the lift at 0.5 m. Compare one supporting rope section with two; change nothing else.
experiments.observe: Ideal pulling force changes from 392.4 N to 196.2 N while rope travel changes from 0.5 m to 1.0 m. Ideal input work and the load's gravitational energy gain both stay 196.2 J. Explain why less force requires more rope.

experiments.title: Change only driven gear teeth
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Keep the driver at 12 teeth, the load at 40 kg, the lift at 0.5 m and both crank and drum radii at 0.20 m. Compare 12 with 48 driven teeth; change nothing else.
experiments.observe: Crank turns change from 0.40 to 1.59 while ideal hand force changes from 392.4 N to 98.1 N. Ideal work stays 196.2 J. Explain why the larger driven gear requires more hand travel.

misconception: A machine does not remove the minimum energy transfer for a lift. It trades force for distance in the ideal model; real losses make actual input work greater than useful output work.

sources.title: OpenStax: Mechanical advantage and work in simple machines
UC San Diego MAE: Gear ratios
NASA Glenn: Work, force and distance

title: Heat House
subject: Physics
summary: Compare wall and window heat-transfer power, then track how transferred energy accumulates at fixed temperatures.
question: How do wall insulation, window area and elapsed time change heat-transfer power and energy when temperatures stay fixed?
explanation: Thermal energy transfers from warmer places toward cooler places. Power is the rate of energy transfer in watts (joules per second); energy transferred over time is reported in joules, megajoules and kilowatt-hours. Insulation adds thermal resistance and slows transfer through the wall path; it does not create thermal energy. Real buildings transfer energy by conduction through materials, convection with moving fluids and radiation by electromagnetic waves. This steady-state model folds assembly effects into fixed U-factors instead of calculating those mechanisms separately. It holds both temperatures steady, treats added windows as replacements for opaque wall inside a 60 m² envelope, and omits the roof, floor, air leaks, sunlight, moisture, thermal bridges, stored heat and equipment. The values are teaching inputs, not measurements, product ratings, a weather forecast or an energy-bill estimate.

experiments.title: Wall insulation
experiments.instruction: Predict what happens to window heat-transfer power. Set the baseline at brick, 8 m² windows, 20°C inside, 0°C outside, 6 h and 0 cm added insulation. Then change only added insulation to 10 cm.
experiments.observe: Wall power falls from 2066 W to 346 W while window power stays 448 W. Over 6 h, combined transferred energy falls from 15.09 kWh to 4.77 kWh. Explain why changing the wall path leaves the unchanged window path fixed.

experiments.title: Window area
experiments.instruction: Predict what happens to combined outward power. Set the baseline at brick, 10 cm insulation, 20°C inside, 0°C outside, 6 h and 2 m² windows. Then change only window area to 18 m²; windows replace wall inside the same envelope.
experiments.observe: Opaque wall area falls from 58 to 42 m², combined power rises from 498 W to 1288 W, and 6 h energy rises from 2.99 kWh to 7.73 kWh. Explain why both area and U-factor determine this teaching result.

misconception: Insulation does not generate warmth, and watts are not a temperature or an amount of energy. Insulation slows transfer through its path; at constant power, transferred energy still accumulates with elapsed time.

title: Pressure Tank
subject: Physics
summary: Change water height or tank shape and compare head, wall-sensor pressure, net force and ideal outlet speed.
question: What sets static pressure on a wall sensor and ideal jet speed from a separate nozzle in an open water tank?
explanation: In still water of fixed density, static gauge pressure on the separate closed wall sensor grows directly with vertical depth below the surface: gauge pressure = density × gravitational acceleration × head. Absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure. Gauge pressure times the fixed 100 cm² area gives sensor net force because its opposite face is exposed to atmosphere. The nozzle is separate; its emerging free jet is approximately atmospheric. For an open tank with a small horizontal outlet, the same head sets ideal initial speed through √(2gh). A wider tank stores more water but does not change equal-head pressure, sensor net force or ideal speed. Range also depends on how long the horizontal jet falls from the outlet to floor level. The model holds the level fixed at one instant and omits draining, viscosity, turbulence, outlet contraction, air drag, splashing, wall stresses, temperature-dependent density and sealed-gas or pump effects. Calculated values use displayed teaching constants; dimensions and standard atmosphere are teaching inputs, not measurements, equipment specifications or operating guidance.

experiments.title: Raise the water
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Set the surface to 1 m in the narrow tank with the outlet fixed at 0.5 m, then change only the surface to 2 m.
experiments.observe: Head rises from 0.5 to 1.5 m. Calculated gauge pressure and net force on the fixed wall sensor triple, while ideal speed rises by √3. Explain why pressure and speed respond by different factors.

experiments.title: Change tank shape
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Keep the surface at 2 m and outlet at 0.5 m, then change only the tank from narrow to wide. Compare one instant before either tank drains.
experiments.observe: Volume rises from 2,000 to 6,480 L, but head stays 1.5 m. Wall-sensor gauge pressure, sensor net force and ideal speed remain unchanged. Explain why volume alone does not set pressure at that depth.

misconception: More total water does not automatically mean greater pressure at a chosen depth. The closed wall sensor measures static pressure there; the separate emerging free jet is approximately atmospheric. Equal head in the same liquid gives equal static gauge pressure even when tank volume differs.

title: Moving Plates
subject: Earth science
summary: Compare spreading, oceanic–continental subduction and transform motion at equal rates and times, then test a bounded locked-fault illustration.
question: How does the direction plates move change what happens at their boundary?
explanation: A tectonic plate is lithosphere: crust plus rigid uppermost mantle. It moves over hotter, slowly deforming, mostly solid asthenosphere. At a divergent mid-ocean ridge, oceanic lithosphere separates and localized melt can cool into new oceanic crust. In this oceanic–continental convergent example, denser oceanic lithosphere bends beneath continental lithosphere at a trench; melt is localized in the mantle wedge above the slab, not throughout the mantle or entire slab. At a transform boundary, plates move horizontally past one another without creating or destroying crust in this model. The calculation assumes a constant relative rate: 1 cm/yr sustained for 1 million years gives 10 km of relative motion. That arithmetic is exact for the displayed units, but the chosen rates, times, scene dimensions, relief and slab angle are teaching inputs rather than a reconstruction of a named plate boundary. The separate locked-fault illustration uses an invented five-step threshold and 20-slip display limit. It has no time or magnitude scale and cannot predict an earthquake date, location, magnitude or hazard.

experiments.title: Boundary direction
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Compare Apart and Together at 4 cm/yr for 2.0 million years. Change only the boundary example; hold rate, elapsed time and schematic view fixed.
experiments.observe: Both examples calculate 80 km of relative motion. Apart forms a ridge and new oceanic crust; Together forms a trench and carries oceanic lithosphere beneath continental lithosphere. Explain why equal relative motion can build different structures.

experiments.title: Locked fault slip
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Start Sideways after four equal loading steps, then add only the fifth step. Hold the boundary, long-term rate and elapsed model time fixed.
experiments.observe: The invented loading index drops from 80% to 0%, the illustrated slip count changes from 0 to 1 and the surface marker gains one schematic offset. Explain why this timeless five-step illustration is not an earthquake clock or hazard forecast.

misconception: Tectonic plates are not crust alone, and the mantle is not a global ocean of liquid magma. Plates continue moving between earthquakes; earthquakes can occur at all boundary types and within plates. A regular schematic slip sequence is not a real earthquake clock.

title: Cloud and Rain Lab
subject: Earth science
summary: Predict, then test how parcel cooling forms a visible cloud and how particle growth and evaporation affect rain at the ground.
question: When does invisible water vapor form a visible cloud, and when does liquid precipitation reach the ground?
explanation: Water vapor is an invisible gas. As a rising parcel expands and cools, its saturation vapor pressure decreases and relative humidity rises. At saturation, some vapor can condense on particles into visible liquid droplets while condensation and evaporation both continue. A warm cloud still needs particle growth—often collision and coalescence—before liquid precipitation falls; a drier layer below cloud can completely evaporate falling drops into virga. Real clouds may contain liquid droplets, ice crystals or both. This bounded warm-cloud teaching model uses one numerical saturation crossing, fixed cooling rates, a chosen representative particle size and an invented evaporation-path coefficient. It is not a forecast.

experiments.title: Lift to saturation
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Start with 400 m of parcel lift, then change only lift to 1,600 m. Hold starting temperature at 24 °C, starting relative humidity at 60%, particle diameter at 20 µm and below-cloud relative humidity at 80%.
experiments.observe: Compare parcel temperature, relative humidity, estimated cloud base and modeled condensate. Explain why cooling to saturation can turn some invisible vapor into visible liquid droplets without producing precipitation-sized particles.

experiments.title: Grow precipitation
experiments.instruction: Predict first. In the same saturated warm cloud, start with 20 µm droplets, then change only representative particle diameter to 1,000 µm. Hold lift, temperature and both relative-humidity settings fixed.
experiments.observe: Compare the unchanged cloud measurements, the particle's 125,000-fold volume change and its estimated diameter at ground level. Explain why cloud particles must grow and why precipitation aloft can evaporate before the ground.

misconception: Air does not literally hold water. Relative humidity compares actual vapor pressure with saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature. A visible cloud consists of liquid droplets, ice crystals or both—not the invisible vapor itself—and not every cloud produces rain at the ground.

title: Magnetic Fields
subject: Physics
summary: Predict, then test how reversing one complete bar changes its interaction and how two nonzero fields can cancel at one exact probe location.
question: How do two complete bar magnets set one compass direction, and when can their fields cancel?
explanation: A compass is a small magnet whose north-seeking end aligns with the local magnetic field. Outside a bar magnet, conventional field direction runs from its north pole toward its south pole. Fields from both bars combine by vector addition, so a compass responds to the local sum rather than simply choosing the nearest pole. Unlike facing poles attract and like facing poles repel. In this model, equal opposing contributions cancel at the exact midpoint between like facing poles, but each magnet still produces a field elsewhere. The bars are represented by paired softened signed sources only to approximate the exterior tabletop field; these are not isolated magnetic poles. The 0–100 field index and diagram-unit distances are normalized comparisons, not tesla, metres, force measurements or a prediction of magnet motion.

experiments.title: Reverse one magnet
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Start with N–S facing, then reverse only the right magnet to make N–N face. Hold the 2-unit gap, probe position (0, 2) and identical bars fixed.
experiments.observe: N–S facing poles attract; N–N facing poles repel. Compare the north-seeking direction and normalized field index. Explain why reversing one complete bar changes both its pole labels and its contribution to the combined field.

experiments.title: Test cancellation
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Keep N–N poles facing at gap 2. Start with the probe at (0, 0), then change only probe z to 2. Hold both magnets and probe x fixed.
experiments.observe: At the exact midpoint, two equal nonzero contributions oppose and the normalized combined index is 0, so there is no preferred direction. Away from the midpoint the combined field is nonzero. Explain why cancellation at one point does not switch off either magnet.

misconception: Field lines are a mapping tool, not material threads, flowing substance or particle paths. For a real magnet they form closed loops, including through the magnet; the displayed exterior lines and their spacing are illustrative.

title: Cell Explorer
subject: Biology
summary: Inspect plant and animal cell structures, then compare how oxygen and glucose cross a model membrane.
question: Why can a concentration difference move one substance across a membrane but not another?
explanation: Plant and animal cells share structures such as a cell membrane, nucleus and mitochondria. This green plant-cell example also has chloroplasts, a cell wall and a large central vacuole; many non-green plant cells lack chloroplasts. A selectively permeable membrane allows some substances through more easily than others. Oxygen diffuses through the model’s lipid layer, while glucose needs a carrier protein. Equal-sized compartments, relative concentration units and fixed transfer steps simplify the comparison; active transport and metabolism are omitted.

experiments.title: Same gradient, different molecules
experiments.instruction: Start with outside concentration 12, inside concentration 4 and no glucose carrier. Predict the difference between oxygen and glucose. Transfer oxygen for one step, restore both starting concentrations, then choose glucose and transfer one step.
experiments.observe: Oxygen moves down its concentration gradient, while glucose does not cross this model membrane without a carrier. Explain why a concentration difference alone does not ensure passage.

experiments.title: Provide a selective pathway
experiments.instruction: Choose glucose, restore outside concentration 12 and inside concentration 4, and leave the carrier absent. Predict the effect of adding the glucose carrier, then compare one transfer step without it and one with it, restoring the starting concentrations between trials.
experiments.observe: With the carrier, glucose moves from higher to lower concentration while the total amount stays the same. Explain why this is passive transport rather than a pump moving material against its gradient.

misconception: Plant cells have mitochondria as well as any chloroplasts they contain. A cell wall is outside the membrane, not a replacement for its selective control of transport.

title: Shape Slicer
subject: Mathematics
summary: Rotate a cube, tetrahedron or sphere, move a slicing plane and compare the resulting cross sections.
question: Can the same solid make different cross-section shapes?
explanation: A cross section is where a solid meets a flat plane. Rotating a solid relative to the plane or moving the plane can change the section. Changing only the viewing angle does not change the actual section. A tetrahedron has four triangular faces. A cube can make several section polygons; a sphere’s non-tangent plane sections are circles of different sizes. This model uses ideal solids and reports area and boundary length in model units. A flat section has no thickness, unlike a physical slice.

experiments.title: A cube is not always square inside
experiments.instruction: Choose the cube with tilt 0°, turn 0° and slice offset 0. Predict the section made by the Diagonal cube slice preset, then compare it with the starting section.
experiments.observe: The face-parallel center slice is a square, while the diagonal center slice is a hexagon. Compare the number of intersected faces and explain why a cube’s square faces do not force every section to be square.

experiments.title: Move a plane through a sphere
experiments.instruction: Choose the sphere and keep its orientation fixed. Predict how the section changes when slice offset moves from 0 to 0.6, then compare the radius and area.
experiments.observe: The radius decreases from 1 to 0.8 units and the area falls to 64% of the central section’s area. Explain why both sections remain circles even though their sizes differ.

misconception: A cross section is not a solid’s shadow or outer silhouette. A plane that misses the solid makes no section; a tangent plane can meet a sphere at just one point.

title: Adaptation Island
subject: Biology
summary: Change a habitat and follow inherited shell colors through generations of a model population.
question: How can a population change over generations without individuals choosing new traits?
explanation: Individuals can differ in inherited traits. In this fictional population, predators are less likely to find shells that blend with the ground. Surviving individuals contribute offspring with the same shell-color type, so the proportions can change across generations. Individuals do not change their own shell color. The model shows deterministic expected percentages using invented survival weights, not sampled animal counts. It holds population size constant and omits mutation, migration, chance and other traits.

experiments.title: Compare two habitats
experiments.instruction: Start with 50% dark shells and predators present. Predict the five-generation trend on dark ground and on light ground. Run each habitat for five generations, using Reset population before the second run to restore the same starting mix.
experiments.observe: Different shell colors become more common in the two habitats. Explain the change through inherited variation and different survival, rather than individuals choosing the color they need.

experiments.title: Remove this selection pressure
experiments.instruction: Use dark ground and a starting dark-shell share of 50%. Predict how removing predators changes the trend. Compare five generations with predators and five without, restarting to the same initial mix before each run.
experiments.observe: Without predators, both colors have equal survival weights and their expected proportions stay fixed in this model. Explain why inherited variation alone did not produce the same trend as variation with unequal survival.

misconception: Natural selection does not plan ahead, create a needed trait on demand or guarantee progress. It changes the frequency of existing inherited variants under particular conditions.
